newsitem.title: FRANCE: French row grows over Mitterrand bugging secrecy.
newsitem.headline: French row grows over Mitterrand bugging secrecy.

text.p: Even from beyond the grave, Francois Mitterrand continues to overshadow French politics.
Indeed leading cartoonist Plantu of Le Monde has taken to depicting the late Socialist president listening in on his successors through a set of headphones from a cloud in heaven.

The disclosure last week that Mitterrand, who died in January 1996 seven months after completing 14 years in power, personally oversaw the illegal wiretapping of dozens of politicians, journalists and lawyers has sparked public outrage.

At first sight, the scandal is an acute embarrassment for his Socialist party in the run-up to a general election due next March. But it could also cause problems for the wily old ruler's conservative successors.

Politicians of the left and right have united, with rare exceptions, to criticise Gaullist Prime Minister Alain Juppe for refusing to lift official secrecy surrounding the so-called "Elysee Palace bugging affair".
Gaullist back-bencher Alain Marsaud, a former anti-terrorist magistrate, said: "The prime minister would be well advised to lift official secrecy today because citizens expect the truth."

The "defence secrecy" officially invoked seems harder to justify now that documents published by Le Monde and L'Express magazine suggest some of the bugging was done to conceal the existence of Mitterrand's illegitimate daughter, Mazarine.

Juppe's supporters are trying to focus public attention on what they see as the "real scandal" -- that a head of state who purported to embody republican virtue illegally snooped on innocent citizens -- rather than on the unexplained reasons why the government is using state secrecy to withhold evidence from a judge investigating the matter.
While Mitterrand was never held to account for the illegal telephone-tapping between 1982 and 1986, the affair seems likely to keep French courts busy for several years.
Former presidential aides and members of a rogue anti-terror squad that worked directly for Mitterrand face prosecution for invasion of privacy and civil lawsuits by some wiretap victims.
By comparison, the Watergate scandal which toppled U.S. president Richard Nixon in 1974 over a bungled attempt to bug Democratic party headquarters, looks like a beginner's offence.
France's official watchdog on wire-tapping, Paul Bouchet, on Tuesday joined a chorus urging Juppe to lift official secrecy at least partially.

Bouchet, who heads a National Control Commission on Security Intercepts, told the newspaper Liberation: "What is abnormal is the disloyal use of wiretaps by the Elysee's anti-terrorist cell which deviated from protecting the public interest to protecting a private interest."
Only the identity of officials working for the government's communications interception centre need be shielded, he said.

Mitterrand's outspoken former confidant and budget minister Michel Charasse has been almost his sole defender, saying the late president was entirely justified, in a period of terrorist attacks and blackmail threats, in tapping journalists' and lawyers' telephones.

When Socialist leader Lionel Jospin tried to distance the party from the seamy side of Mitterrand's rule, calling for "monarchical secrecy" to be lifted, Charasse said he should not "betray a sense of state" if he hoped to govern France.

The affair has sparked controversy over who eavesdropped on whom before Mitterrand was elected in 1981 and fuelled suspicion that illegal bugging may continue today despite legal restrains imposed in 1991.

Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who served as president from 1974 to 1981, angrily denied broadcast allegations by a former head of Mitterrand's private office, Jean Glavany, that he had systematically spied on Mitterrand and other opposition leaders.

"On entering the presidency, I took the necessary measures so there would be no wiretaps other than those requested by judges. I took practical steps to ensure periodically that this rule was strictly respected," Giscard d'Estaing said.

"Neither Francois Mitterrand, nor (then Communist leader) Georges Marchais, nor any other politician or journalist was the object of wiretaps ordered by the Elysee from 1974 to 1981," he added in a statement, threatening to sue anyone who stated the contrary.
